about: Hand-written grammar-correction exercises (original sentences), levelled along the CEFR progression. Each 'wrong' differs from 'correct' by one change of at most three words (tests/test_grammar.py enforces this).

items.correct: My sister works in a hospital.
items.wrong: My sister work in a hospital.
items.why: With he, she, it or a singular noun, the present simple adds -s: works.

items.correct: They are very happy today.
items.wrong: They is very happy today.
items.why: With they, be is are: they are.

items.correct: We have three children and two dogs.
items.wrong: We have three child and two dogs.
items.why: After a number above one, use the plural: children (child is irregular).

items.correct: Those books are very interesting.
items.wrong: Those book are very interesting.
items.why: Those points to more than one thing, so the noun is plural: books.

items.correct: Does your brother like football?
items.wrong: Do your brother like football?
items.why: Questions about he, she, it or a singular noun use does.

items.correct: He doesn't eat meat.
items.wrong: He don't eat meat.
items.why: With he, she or it the negative is doesn't.

items.correct: She is an engineer at a big company.
items.wrong: She is a engineer at a big company.
items.why: Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an engineer.

items.correct: It takes an hour to get there.
items.wrong: It takes a hour to get there.
items.why: The h in hour is silent, so it starts with a vowel sound: an hour.

items.correct: Yesterday I went to the cinema with my friends.
items.wrong: Yesterday I goed to the cinema with my friends.
items.why: Go is irregular: the past simple is went.

items.correct: She bought a new phone last week.
items.wrong: She buyed a new phone last week.
items.why: Buy is irregular: the past simple is bought.

items.correct: We ate dinner at eight o'clock.
items.wrong: We eated dinner at eight o'clock.
items.why: Eat is irregular: the past simple is ate.

items.correct: I was born in 1995.
items.wrong: I was born on 1995.
items.why: Years take in: in 1995 (days take on, times take at).

items.correct: The meeting is on Monday morning.
items.wrong: The meeting is in Monday morning.
items.why: Days, even with a part of the day, take on: on Monday morning.

items.correct: She is very good at maths.
items.wrong: She is very good in maths.
items.why: The fixed expression is good at something.

items.correct: My new flat is bigger than the old one.
items.wrong: My new flat is more big than the old one.
items.why: Short adjectives add -er: bigger, not more big.

items.correct: This is the best pizza in town.
items.wrong: This is the most good pizza in town.
items.why: Good is irregular: good, better, the best.

items.correct: I saw that film last weekend.
items.wrong: I have seen that film last weekend.
items.why: A finished time (last weekend) needs the past simple: I saw.

items.correct: I have lived in London since 2018.
items.wrong: I live in London since 2018.
items.why: Something that started in the past and still goes on (since 2018) takes the present perfect: I have lived.

items.correct: We have known each other for ten years.
items.wrong: We know each other for ten years.
items.why: With for + a period up to now, use the present perfect: we have known.

items.correct: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
items.wrong: If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
items.why: After if, use the present for the future: if it rains.

items.correct: I'll call you when I arrive.
items.wrong: I'll call you when I will arrive.
items.why: After when, use the present for the future: when I arrive.

items.correct: I enjoy swimming in the sea.
items.wrong: I enjoy to swim in the sea.
items.why: Enjoy is followed by the -ing form: enjoy swimming.

items.correct: She decided to study medicine.
items.wrong: She decided studying medicine.
items.why: Decide is followed by to + infinitive: decided to study.

items.correct: I used to play the piano when I was a child.
items.wrong: I use to play the piano when I was a child.
items.why: For past habits the form is used to: I used to play.

items.correct: If I had more money, I would buy a house.
items.wrong: If I would have more money, I would buy a house.
items.why: In the if-clause of an unreal condition use the past simple, not would: if I had.

items.correct: If I were you, I would accept the offer.
items.wrong: If I would be you, I would accept the offer.
items.why: Giving advice uses if I were you, never if I would be.

items.correct: I wish I had more free time.
items.wrong: I wish I have more free time.
items.why: Wish about the present takes a past form: I wish I had.

items.correct: I wish I could speak Japanese.
items.wrong: I wish I can speak Japanese.
items.why: Wish about the present takes a past form: I wish I could.

items.correct: The bridge was built in 1890.
items.wrong: The bridge was build in 1890.
items.why: The passive is be + past participle: was built.

items.correct: English is spoken all over the world.
items.wrong: English is speaking all over the world.
items.why: The passive is be + past participle: is spoken.

items.correct: I'm looking forward to seeing you.
items.wrong: I'm looking forward to see you.
items.why: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it takes the -ing form: to seeing.

items.correct: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.
items.wrong: Despite of the rain, we went for a walk.
items.why: Despite takes no of (in spite of does).

items.correct: If I had known, I would have called you.
items.wrong: If I would have known, I would have called you.
items.why: For an unreal past condition use if + past perfect: if I had known.

items.correct: If they had left earlier, they wouldn't have missed the train.
items.wrong: If they would have left earlier, they wouldn't have missed the train.
items.why: For an unreal past condition use if + past perfect: if they had left.

items.correct: If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.
items.wrong: If she would have studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.
items.why: The if-clause about the past takes the past perfect: if she had studied.

items.correct: I'd rather you didn't smoke in here.
items.wrong: I'd rather you don't smoke in here.
items.why: Would rather + another person takes a past form for the present: I'd rather you didn't.

items.correct: It's high time we went home.
items.wrong: It's high time we go home.
items.why: It's high time takes a past form: it's high time we went.

items.correct: The man whose car was stolen called the police.
items.wrong: The man who's car was stolen called the police.
items.why: Whose shows possession; who's means who is.

items.correct: No sooner had I sat down than the phone rang.
items.wrong: No sooner had I sat down when the phone rang.
items.why: No sooner is always paired with than.

items.correct: The number of students has increased this year.
items.wrong: The number of students have increased this year.
items.why: The subject is the number (singular), not students: has increased.

items.correct: She has worked here since January.
items.wrong: She works here since January.
items.why: Since + a starting point takes the present perfect: she has worked.

items.correct: We went to Spain two years ago.
items.wrong: We have gone to Spain two years ago.
items.why: Ago marks a finished time, so it takes the past simple: we went.

items.correct: As soon as I get home, I'll call you.
items.wrong: As soon as I will get home, I'll call you.
items.why: After as soon as, use the present for the future: as soon as I get home.

items.correct: He finished writing the report at midnight.
items.wrong: He finished to write the report at midnight.
items.why: Finish is followed by the -ing form: finished writing.

items.correct: I hope to see you soon.
items.wrong: I hope seeing you soon.
items.why: Hope is followed by to + infinitive: hope to see.

items.correct: Did you use to live in Paris?
items.wrong: Did you used to live in Paris?
items.why: After did, the form is use to: did you use to live.

items.correct: I'm not used to getting up early.
items.wrong: I'm not used to get up early.
items.why: In be used to, to is a preposition, so it takes the -ing form: used to getting up.

items.correct: It depends on the weather.
items.wrong: It depends of the weather.
items.why: Depend takes on: it depends on.

items.correct: If she knew the answer, she would tell us.
items.wrong: If she would know the answer, she would tell us.
items.why: In the if-clause of an unreal condition use the past simple, not would: if she knew.

items.correct: What would you do if you won the lottery?
items.wrong: What would you do if you would win the lottery?
items.why: In the if-clause of an unreal condition use the past simple, not would: if you won.

items.correct: I wish you were here.
items.wrong: I wish you are here.
items.why: Wish about the present takes a past form: I wish you were here.

items.correct: The letters were sent yesterday.
items.wrong: The letters were send yesterday.
items.why: The passive is be + past participle: were sent.

items.correct: This house was designed by a famous architect.
items.wrong: This house was design by a famous architect.
items.why: The passive is be + past participle: was designed.

items.correct: He suggested going to the cinema.
items.wrong: He suggested to go to the cinema.
items.why: Suggest is followed by the -ing form (or that + clause): suggested going.

items.correct: Although it was late, we kept talking.
items.wrong: Although it was late, but we kept talking.
items.why: Although already links the two ideas, so but is not needed.

items.correct: You'd better take an umbrella.
items.wrong: You'd better to take an umbrella.
items.why: Had better is followed by the bare infinitive: you'd better take.

items.correct: If we had booked earlier, we would have got a better price.
items.wrong: If we would have booked earlier, we would have got a better price.
items.why: For an unreal past condition use if + past perfect: if we had booked.
also: If we had booked earlier, we would have gotten a better price.

items.correct: Had I known, I would have helped.
items.wrong: Had I knew, I would have helped.
items.why: Had I known is the inverted form of if I had known: had + past participle.
also: If I had known, I would have helped.

items.correct: It's about time you found a job.
items.wrong: It's about time you find a job.
items.why: It's about time takes a past form: it's about time you found.

items.correct: I wish I had gone to the party.
items.wrong: I wish I went to the party.
items.why: A regret about the past takes the past perfect: I wish I had gone.

items.correct: Hardly had I arrived when it started raining.
items.wrong: Hardly had I arrived than it started raining.
items.why: Hardly is paired with when (no sooner is paired with than).

items.correct: The more you practise, the better you get.
items.wrong: The more you practise, the more better you get.
items.why: Better is already a comparative: the better you get.

items.correct: Would you mind opening the window?
items.wrong: Would you mind to open the window?
items.why: Mind is followed by the -ing form: would you mind opening.

items.correct: It was such a good film that we watched it twice.
items.wrong: It was so a good film that we watched it twice.
items.why: Such goes before a + adjective + noun; so goes before an adjective alone.
